text: Everything up to now has lived inside Snowflake. This lesson connects the tool the VP of Support will actually open: Power BI, pointed directly at the view.

In Power BI Desktop, get data, more, Snowflake. Enter the account identifier and the warehouse, support underscore w h. Sign in as the support analyst role — the same role built and granted access back in lessons six and seven, never an admin account, just because it's convenient. Then, in the navigator, pick the daily ticket summary view. Not the raw tickets table.

That choice is the whole payoff of the last two lessons. The view already has the right grain and the right scope for this month baked in. Connect to the raw table instead, and every single visual in the report would need its own group-by logic written in DAX, duplicating work that's already correct in one place.

One more decision: import mode, or DirectQuery. Import copies the view's current result into Power BI's own model — fast to work with, but a snapshot until it's refreshed. DirectQuery sends a live query to Snowflake every single time a visual changes — always current, but slower, and it keeps the warehouse running more.

For this project, import is the right call. The data is tiny, and this is a report a VP checks once before a Monday meeting — not a dashboard dozens of people are hammering in real time. DirectQuery earns its cost once you actually need minute-by-minute freshness, or the data's too big to copy. Neither is true here.
The report is connected, loaded, and ready. Next lesson, we take it back to the person who asked for it in the first place — presenting the finished report to the VP of Support.
